Funny, shrugging, sad - Lipman was born to play this exhausting feat of a part.

Her story mixes sadness with a good deal of humour and is performed brilliantly by Maureen Lipman, whose every gesture, every facial expression and every phrasing of some thoughtful, often witty comment is absolutely riveting. She admits that, “nowadays, breathing is one of the few pleasures I have left.” The monologue divides into three sections.
There's real magic to this play, and it's no surprise it has seen such success.

“That”, she briskly points out, “is an irony not lost on me”. It is a gentle piece of sardonic wit, one of many in Sherman’s pithy script, delivered with unexpected restraint by a melancholy and vividly reflective Maureen Lipman.
Lipman renders Rose's inner dichotomies with understated yet astonishing detail, a Japanese netsuke sculpture humbly glistening on stage.
Maureen Lipman is quietly charismatic in this role, almost making one forget the imperfections in the writing, which veers towards the self-indulgent, especially in the over-long Act Two.

cn.t: Lipman delivers a commanding performance in Sherman's Holocaust monologue, holding the stage for over two hours. Critics praise her stamina and range, though some find the sprawling memory play uneven.
